r:bipProKopf:name: Economic prosperity per capita
r:bipProKopf:beschreibung: Real GDP per inhabitant at start-year prices. The average, not what reaches the individual.
r:bipProKopf:info:0: Economic output (GDP) divided by the number of inhabitants, at start-year prices. Inflation is therefore taken out.
r:bipProKopf:info:1: The simplest measure of economic prosperity: how much is produced per capita? It is an average. How income is distributed is shown in the chart on inequality (Gini). The figure does not measure life satisfaction, quality of life or the state of the environment.
r:bipProKopf:info:2: The G7 grow by about 1% a year in the long run, with ageing more like 0.5 to 1%. Below 0.5% counts as stagnation. A fall of more than 0.5% is a recession; three years of decline in a row or more than 10% below the peak are a depression.
r:bipProKopf:info:3: Productivity times people in work, divided by inhabitants. Productivity grows with research, start-ups and cheap energy.
r:schuldQuote:name: Government debt
r:schuldQuote:beschreibung: Debt ratio. The red line marks 90%, where markets get nervous. Negative means: the state has more assets than debt.
r:schuldQuote:info:0: Government debt relative to one year's economic output.
r:schuldQuote:info:1: Shows how heavy the burden is relative to the strength to carry it. High debt makes a country vulnerable to rising interest rates.
r:schuldQuote:info:2: Maastricht limit 60%. From about 90%, markets get nervous about countries without their own central bank. Japan carries over 250% because it prints its own currency.
r:schuldQuote:info:3: Debt grows with interest and deficits and shrinks relatively through growth. What matters is whether the interest rate is above growth (r − g).
r:alq:name: Unemployment
r:alq:beschreibung: Share of the labour force without work.
r:alq:info:0: Share of the labour force looking for work and not finding it.
r:alq:info:1: Unemployment costs income, taxes and contributions and strains the social funds twice.
r:alq:info:2: Below 4% counts as full employment, above 10% as a crisis.
r:alq:info:3: Rises when growth falls below trend (Okun's law). On top come shocks and, in the short run, harsh austerity.
r:inflation:name: Inflation
r:inflation:beschreibung: Price rise per year. Central bank target: 2%.
r:inflation:info:0: How much consumer prices rise per year.
r:inflation:info:1: Too much inflation eats wages and savings. Falling prices (deflation) paralyse investment and make debt heavier.
r:inflation:info:2: Central banks target 2%. Above 4% the economy counts as overheated, below 0% deflation threatens.
r:inflation:info:3: Expected inflation plus capacity use plus energy prices. With a hard currency there is no inflation target; growth then pushes prices down.
r:aufschlag:name: Risk premium
r:aufschlag:beschreibung: Premium on the government bond over a safe borrower. Above 3 percentage points a crisis threatens.
r:aufschlag:info:0: The extra interest a state has to pay compared with a safe borrower, in percentage points.
r:aufschlag:info:1: This is how the market measures the risk of default. If the premium rises, every new debt gets dearer, and a spiral can begin.
r:aufschlag:info:2: Below 1 percentage point is relaxed. Above 3 percentage points a crisis threatens. Italy was at about 5.5 in 2011.
r:aufschlag:info:3: A curve over the debt ratio, plus foreign debt, primary deficit and, without a protection scheme, panic. How steep it is depends on the currency regime. The ECB protection scheme (TPI) dampens it.
r:energiepreis:name: Energy price
r:energiepreis:info:0: Index of the energy price for industry, start year = 100.
r:energiepreis:info:1: Energy is in almost everything. Expensive energy drives inflation and drives away energy-intensive industry such as chemicals, steel and glass.
r:energiepreis:info:2: If the value stays above 150, energy-intensive industry is at risk.
r:energiepreis:info:3: Cost of the energy mix plus CO₂ price plus world prices for oil and gas. Fast expansion of renewables lowers the price in the long run.
r:beschaeftigte:name: People in work
r:beschaeftigte:beschreibung: People in work as part of the total population. The light block is all inhabitants.
r:beschaeftigte:info:0: Everyone in paid work, compared with the number of inhabitants.
r:beschaeftigte:info:1: People in work also carry children, pensioners and the unemployed. If their share falls, the burden per capita gets heavier.
r:beschaeftigte:info:2: Germany is at about 55% today. Below 48% the burden becomes clearly noticeable.
r:beschaeftigte:info:3: Population by age, plus retirement age and migration. For migration, skills and speed of integration count.
r:rentenausgaben:name: Pension spending
r:rentenausgaben:info:0: Public spending on pensions as a percentage of economic output.
r:rentenausgaben:info:1: This is the largest single item of the welfare state, and it grows automatically with ageing.
r:rentenausgaben:info:2: Germany is at about 10% today, Italy at about 16%.
r:rentenausgaben:info:3: Pensioners times pension level times average wage. A funded system costs double at first and relieves later.
r:primaer:name: Primary balance
r:primaer:beschreibung: Budget balance excluding interest. Positive means surplus.
r:primaer:info:0: Government revenue minus spending, excluding interest payments.
r:primaer:info:1: Shows whether the state covers its current tasks from its own strength.
r:primaer:info:2: If the interest rate is above growth, a surplus is needed to keep the debt ratio from rising.
r:primaer:info:3: Taxes (with Laffer effect) minus government spending, pensions, defence and the cost of shocks. A debt brake counter-steers.
r:spielraum:name: Budget headroom
r:spielraum:beschreibung: What remains of government revenue after interest, pensions and social spending are paid.
r:spielraum:info:0: Of 100 units of government revenue, interest, pensions and health, families and the unemployed are deducted. The rest remains for everything else: defence, education, research, infrastructure, police, administration.
r:spielraum:info:1: If interest and pension burdens grow, they crowd out the other tasks. Then the state must raise taxes, cut services or borrow for everything else.
r:spielraum:info:2: Germany was at about 50 in 2025, the USA at just under 40. Below 10 it becomes critical: almost every other task then depends on new debt. Negative means: interest and social spending alone cost more than the state takes in.
r:spielraum:info:3: Revenue minus interest, pension and social spending, divided by revenue. The model cuts nothing on its own; it only shows how tight it gets. How a state would react is planned (Spec 13.10).
r:leistungsbilanz:name: Current account
r:leistungsbilanz:beschreibung: Exports minus imports plus income from abroad.
r:leistungsbilanz:info:0: Exports minus imports plus income from foreign assets, as % of GDP.
r:leistungsbilanz:info:1: A surplus means the country lends savings abroad. A deficit has to be financed from abroad.
r:leistungsbilanz:info:2: Persistent deficits above 4% make a country vulnerable when capital leaves. Germany has had surpluses of about 5 to 7% for years.
r:leistungsbilanz:info:3: Exports follow world demand, exchange rate and energy price; imports follow domestic demand and the energy bill.
r:co2Mt:name: CO₂ emissions
r:co2Mt:info:0: The country's carbon dioxide emissions in million tonnes per year.
r:co2Mt:info:1: Shows how far the conversion of the energy supply has come.
r:co2Mt:info:2: Germany was at about 650 Mt in 2024; the goal is climate neutrality by 2045.
r:co2Mt:info:3: The power share follows the energy mix, the rest falls with the CO₂ price. Both grow with economic output.
r:gini:name: Income inequality (Gini)
r:gini:beschreibung: How unequally incomes are distributed. Only rough in the model.
r:gini:info:0: The Gini coefficient measures how unequally incomes are distributed: 0 means everyone has the same, 100 means one person has everything. Statistical offices survey households about their income after taxes and social benefits and rank them from poor to rich.
r:gini:info:1: It shows whether growth reaches most people. It measures income, not wealth: wealth is far more unequally distributed (Germany 2023: 72, Bundesbank). Very high incomes are often missing from surveys, so true inequality tends to be higher.
r:gini:info:2: There is no threshold for good or critical; how much inequality is right is a question of values. For orientation: Germany is a little above 30, the USA just under 40. Before taxes and social benefits Germany would be at about 50 (OECD). For seven countries the starting values come from the same source (OECD, disposable income, weighted by household size) and are comparable. China and Russia are measured differently by the World Bank (per person, income or consumption depending on the country); their values are not directly comparable with the others.
r:gini:info:3: Rough: the starting value comes from the country's data. After that it is moved by unemployment, the level of wage replacement, taxes on income, capital income, wealth and inheritance, VAT, family benefits and the pension level. The effect sizes come from a cross-country comparison of OECD data and are listed under assumptions; some rest on thin evidence and can be switched off. Wages, part-time work, household sizes and asset prices do not act on it, so the line tends to show too little movement.
r:vcQuote:name: Venture capital
r:vcQuote:info:0: Venture capital for young firms as % of GDP.
r:vcQuote:info:1: Venture capital creates new firms and products. Per euro it has a stronger effect on productivity than classic research.
r:vcQuote:info:2: Germany is at about 0.07%, the USA at about 0.6%.
r:vcQuote:info:3: Base level plus pension-fund share, dampened by the tax on company sales and barriers to founding. Works with a lag of about 7 years.
r:knappheit:name: Shortage
r:knappheit:beschreibung: Empty shelves caused by price controls. 0 means no shortage.
r:knappheit:info:0: A measure of scarcity of goods: controlled share of the basket times pent-up price pressure. 0 means no shortage.
r:knappheit:info:1: Price controls lower measured inflation, but suppliers deliver less. Queues, black markets and lower production follow.
r:knappheit:info:2: There is no fixed yardstick. Any value above 0 means: part of inflation is only hidden and returns when the controls go.
r:knappheit:info:3: The suppressed part of inflation builds up; when controls are lifted, prices catch up half of it each year. Supply falls by 0.2% per point of shortage.
r:schwarzmarkt:name: Black-market premium
r:schwarzmarkt:beschreibung: How much more foreign currency costs on the black market than at the official rate.
r:schwarzmarkt:info:0: The gap between the official exchange rate and the black-market rate, in percent. Only with a managed currency.
r:schwarzmarkt:info:1: A high premium means the official rate is too dear. Exporters lose, foreign currency gets scarce, capital flees.
r:schwarzmarkt:info:2: Venezuela was above 1,000% in 2015, Argentina at about 150% in 2023. Above 20% counts as a warning sign.
r:schwarzmarkt:info:3: Overvaluation of the official rate against a free shadow rate, times the part of the capital account that is closed. The shadow rate follows interest, current account and capital flight.
r:verdeckteSchuld:name: Hidden debt
r:verdeckteSchuld:beschreibung: Bad loans of state banks not yet counted in government debt.
r:verdeckteSchuld:info:0: Loans that state banks granted on political instruction and that will not be repaid. They are not yet in the official government debt.
r:verdeckteSchuld:info:1: At some point the state must take them over. Then government debt jumps without a visible deficit.
r:verdeckteSchuld:info:2: For China, the IMF estimates the debt of local government financing vehicles at about 50% of GDP. Above 15% counts as a warning sign.
r:verdeckteSchuld:info:3: Part of directed investment turns bad every year. Above the country's threshold (usually 20% of GDP) the state takes the sum into government debt.
r:rohstoffExporte:name: Commodity exports
r:rohstoffExporte:beschreibung: Exports of oil, gas and metals.
r:rohstoffExporte:info:0: Value of exports of oil, gas and metals as % of GDP.
r:rohstoffExporte:info:1: Commodities bring government revenue but create dependence on world prices and buyers. A boom can crowd out other exports (Dutch disease).
r:rohstoffExporte:info:2: Russia is at about 15%, Norway at about 20%. The G7 export hardly any commodities; Canada's energy exports run through the energy balance.
r:rohstoffExporte:info:3: Output times world price index relative to the start, in relation to the rest of the economy, converted at the real exchange rate. Weak rule of law and high state ownership make output decay; sanctions hit less the broader the buyers.
p:arbeit:warum: More people work, fewer draw a pension. That supports growth and the budget at the same time.
p:arbeit:preis: Hardship for physically demanding jobs. Needs exceptions or a flexible transition.
p:fachkraefte:titel: Attract skilled workers and integrate them fast
p:fachkraefte:warum: Young, qualified migration with fast access to the labour market pays in more over a working life than it costs.
p:fachkraefte:preis: Needs housing, language courses and faster recognition of qualifications. That costs money first.
p:gruendungen:warum: More research and venture capital raise productivity. Funded pension schemes supply the money.
p:gruendungen:preis: Works only after 5 to 10 years. Switching to a funded system costs double at first.
p:energie:warum: Fast expansion lowers the energy price in the long run and reduces dependence on imports.
p:energie:preis: High investment in the first years, plus grid and storage expansion.
p:haushalt:warum: Less spending and longer maturities keep the debt ratio and risk premium low. That lowers the interest burden permanently.
p:haushalt:preis: More unemployment in the short run. The cuts hit specific areas.
p:familie:warum: More children today means more people in work in a good 20 years.
p:familie:preis: Works only after a generation and costs immediately. Family policy raises the birth rate only to a limited extent.
p:institutionen:warum: Reliable courts, fewer state enterprises, no price controls and no printing press: investment returns, capital and skilled workers stay.
p:institutionen:preis: Works slowly, over years. Ending price controls first lets the pent-up prices rise.
s:oel:name: Oil price shock
s:oel:txt: Oil and gas become much dearer for two years.
s:krise:name: Financial crisis
s:krise:txt: Banks and credit seize up, capital flees to safe havens.
s:pandemie:name: Pandemic
s:pandemie:txt: Slump in the first year, fast recovery, relief packages, then supply-chain inflation.
s:proxy:name: Proxy war
s:proxy:txt: War in the neighbourhood without own involvement: energy shock, sanctions, rearmament, refugees.
s:krieg:name: War with involvement
s:krieg:txt: Own involvement in war: arms spending up sharply, mobilisation takes workers away, then reconstruction.
s:handel:name: Trade war
s:handel:txt: Tariffs on exports, main buyers buy less.
s:sanktionen:name: Energy supply stop
s:sanktionen:txt: A main supplier stops gas and oil.
s:rohstoffsanktion:name: Sanctions on commodity exports
s:rohstoffsanktion:txt: Buyers purchase less oil, gas and metals.

k:D1:text: About 25 starting values for Germany are set from expert knowledge and not looked up in the original, for example capital coefficient, wage share, NAIRU, net foreign assets, tax bases and power mix. Deviations above 10% are possible. List in quellen.md. Since spec 13.1 a Kalman filter estimates the NAIRU and the productivity trend from the 2000–2025 data with an error band (Assumptions, data situation). For Germany both hand-set values lie within the band of the estimate and stay (NAIRU 3.5 against an estimated 3.2 ± 0.9; productivity trend 0.4 against 0.22 ± 0.24).
k:D1:behebung: Check each value against the source named, correct it in DE-hand.json and mark it as “checked” in quellen.md.
k:D2:text: Rate × base matches revenue, but the base itself is estimated. That distorts the Laffer curves.
k:D2:behebung: Take tax bases from the finance ministry's revenue estimate and official statistics.
k:D5:text: The IMF reports 139% of GDP, BIS-like values are around 110%. The debt-service threshold is therefore adjusted to the model (21 instead of 17).
k:D5:behebung: Use BIS data consistently (credit to the private non-financial sector, debt service ratio).

k:D6:behebung: A traffic light is planned; also include alternative estimates, e.g. night-light studies.
k:D7:titel: Historical data for the backtest unchecked
k:D7:text: World paths 2000–2025 (oil, gas, coal, ECB rate, inflation, world growth, r*), policy paths (tax rates, retirement age, pension level, migration, CO₂ price, ECB purchases) and starting values for 2000 (including government spending without UMTS proceeds) are set from expert knowledge. In the backtest the current account does not start at the actual 2000 value (model 0.3 instead of −1.8% of GDP) because net foreign assets and the energy export share in 2000 are estimated. Since phase 2b there are also paths for NAIRU, participation rate and term premium; the productivity trend 2000–2025 (0.3%) is calibrated to the backtest. Since phase 3a in addition: retirement age in the backtest = actual retirement entry age, census correction 2011 as a separate population adjustment and participation rate, fiscal paths (stimulus packages, price caps, tax reform 2000–2005, financial transactions). These paths are calibration choices: they improve the backtest but are not checked individually against sources.
k:D7:behebung: Add annual values from the World Bank Pink Sheet, ECB Data Portal, Destatis and the finance ministry; file daten/laender/DE-historie.json.
k:M1:text: , from 10.3 to about 15% of GDP by 2050. The model knows no sustainability factor and no link between retirement age and life expectancy. The contribution rate therefore rises by about 8 pp. Official projections are lower. In the backtest pensions rise from 11 to 15% of GDP instead of by 10% in real terms.
k:M1:behebung: Add a sustainability factor as a switch; calibrate against the EU Ageing Report and the pension insurance report.
k:M2:titel: Contribution increases work only through participation
k:M2:text: Non-wage labour costs, undeclared work and emigration do not react.
k:M2:behebung: Add a channel via labour costs and competitiveness.
k:M3:text: Since the mechanism of 29 Sept 2026 the risk premium no longer depends only on the debt level: foreign debt above 60% of GDP (0.03 pp per pp), primary deficit above 3% of GDP (0.25 pp per pp, Laubach 2009) and, with a shared currency without a protection scheme or a hard currency, panic amplification above 5 pp (De Grauwe 2011); a reserve currency protects, managed currencies use their own channel. Greece now opens the valve in 2012, as in the actual haircut. Open: Argentina 2001 under a hard currency does not tip over (premium 2.8 instead of over 40 pp), because the overvaluation came from outside (Brazil's devaluation in 1999, strong dollar) and the model does not know trading partners' exchange rates; Greece's slump stays at −14%, smaller than the observed −25%. Haircut of 50% and monetisation of +8 pp for 3 years remain single-case values. Baseline runs: US debt 2075 358 instead of 336% (eroding reserve status), France 314 instead of 321%, Italy 440 instead of 426%, valve years unchanged; the other countries unchanged. Greece's slump of −14% is just short of the −15% criterion. Since Spec 13.5 part A Argentina reaches the state “crisis” in 2002, but through the credit sawtooth (M30), not through overvaluation; the gap remains.
k:M3:behebung: World path for trading partners' exchange rates (partner devaluation as a shock); check the depth of the slump after a haircut against Greece and Argentina.
k:M4:text: (1 pp of saving per pp of premium) is an assumption with a single source. It may overstate the pressure to save.
k:M4:behebung: Estimate the value from fiscal-reaction studies for several countries; can be switched off as contested.
k:M5:text: are taken from the literature, not estimated for each country.
k:M5:behebung: Calibrate with yield data from 2000 to today for each country (backtest, phase 2).
k:M6:titel: Wealth tax has hardly any downsides
k:M6:text: It has a large base, weak avoidance and is missing from the cost-of-capital wedge for investment.
k:M6:behebung: Include it in the cost-of-capital wedge; elasticity per asset class.
k:M7:text: Mix and price describe electricity; heat and transport are roughly contained in the “remaining CO₂”. The import share scales with the fossil power share.
k:M7:behebung: Add heat and transport sectors; primary energy balance.
k:M8:text: fixed fuel conversions, integration costs quadratic in the renewable share.
k:M9:text: The elasticity to world demand (0.3) is set so that the export ratio stays plausible, not estimated.
k:M10:text: R&D return 0.2 and venture capital factor 3.5 each come from a single study; the range in the literature is wide.
k:M10:behebung: Show the range (band instead of line) or use meta-studies.
k:M11:text: (0.8), independent of interest rates, business cycle and regime.
k:M11:behebung: State-dependent multiplier (higher at the lower bound).
k:M12:text: Normal credit expansion follows trend growth; that prevents an artificial oscillation but smooths real booms. Tested in Spec 13.5 part A (Macrohistory database, 18 countries): credit follows the output gap (+0.45 pp of GDP per % gap), but built in, it creates no boom because the loop dies out, and the German hindcast gets worse. Therefore not adopted. Adopted is the other half: a fall in credit hits demand harder than a rise (factor 1.2, measured 1.42). Since Spec 13.6 a credit boom arises via house prices when the basic setting “Housing and banks” is on: cheap money lifts prices and credit together (USA 2000–2006 almost as measured). It is off by default; then this point holds unchanged.
k:M12:wirkung: medium (by default credit booms and banking crises are missing)
k:M12:behebung: Partly fixed with Spec 13.6 (optional). For the default, the gaps M31–M33 have to be closed first.
k:M14:text: remain rough approximations. Since spec 13.13, taxes, family benefits and the pension level act alongside unemployment and wage replacement, with effect sizes from a cross-country comparison of OECD data. Five of the seven rest on thin evidence (family benefits for the Gini, capital and wealth, VAT, pension level). Social contributions do not act on the Gini. Wages, part-time work, household sizes and asset prices are missing: the lookback does not reproduce the rise of the German Gini in 2000–2005.
k:M14:behebung: Distribution model (income deciles) or calibration against EU-SILC.
k:B1:text: (no mortality, no return migration). All migrants count as of working age, including children on arrival. With very high migration the native working-age population is underestimated.
k:B1:behebung: Track cohorts by age; add a return-migration rate.
k:B2:titel: Emigration of the skilled is a fixed number
k:B2:text: , not a rate. Over 100 years with a shrinking population this becomes extreme.
k:B2:behebung: Model it as a rate of the working-age population.
k:B3:text: , without infant mortality. Life expectancies above about 99 years cannot be represented (the value is silently capped).
k:B3:behebung: Official life table as the base, Gompertz only for the trend.
k:B4:titel: Births along a fixed bell curve
k:B5:text: People who move abroad in retirement (weather, cost of living) keep drawing a pension but no longer consume at home. The model does not know this outflow: demand depends on government spending, interest and credit, not on the population's consumption. Simply removing pensioners from the population would be wrong, because pension spending would then fall too.
k:B5:behebung: Book pensions paid abroad as an outflow in the current account (secondary income), keep pensioners in the pension calculation; figures from the pension insurer's statistics on pensions abroad.
k:B6:titel: Migration values other than net migration are German
k:B6:text: Each country has its own net migration. Everything else is taken from Germany: skills mix, migration routes, target employment rates (82/70/55%), waiting times, speed and cost of integration, age on arrival. For immigration countries with a points system such as Canada this underestimates migrant employment; for countries with long work bans it may overestimate it.
k:B6:behebung: Enter country values from the OECD International Migration Outlook and the OECD/EU Indicators of Immigrant Integration in the respective *-hand.json under standards.
k:U2:titel: Uncertainty band only for random shocks, not for the effect sizes
k:U2:text: Since Spec 13.4 the chart shows a band from 200 runs with random shocks. The ranges of the effect sizes are not included: each effect size still computes with a point value. The band is therefore too narrow. Check against the hindcast for Germany 2000–2025 without the set shocks: measured growth lies within the band in 68% of years (target 80%), unemployment in 72%, government debt only in 36% and the current account never, because there the line itself is off (M17, M20).
k:U2:wirkung: medium (perception: the band looks more precise than the model is)
k:U2:behebung: In the random runs also draw the contested effect sizes from their range; add the ranges to the directory.
k:T1:titel: Backtest: two measures weak, four miss the band target
k:T1:text: Result 2000 → 2025 for Germany after phase 3a (share of years in band · Theil's U against “everything stays” · verdict): GDP growth 68% · 0.70 · target met; inflation 80% · 0.80 · target met; unemployment rate 64% · 0.53 · target narrowly missed; debt ratio 44% · 1.25 · hurdle missed (known weakness, spec 11); population 84% · 0.53 · target met; labour force 28% · 0.15 · target missed (very narrow band, small error); pension spending 36% · 0.99 · target missed, hurdle narrowly met; current account 8% · 0.94 · target missed, direction right, level 2015–2025 too low; yield 68% · 0.43 · target met.
k:T1:behebung: Debt: special measures (bank rescues, zero rates, aid) are not standard mechanics, see M17. Current account: M20. Pension spending: D10. Model inflation is about 1 pp above actual in 2004–2018 (M21).
k:T2:text: The check “stacked shocks tip over” is guaranteed by the shock table, and an exact cash-flow check of the pension fund is missing.
k:U5:titel: Comparison does not read saved scenarios live
k:U5:text: If a saved scenario is overwritten or deleted while selected in the comparison, the comparison shows old figures until the next switch. Newly saved ones appear only after a redraw. If browser storage is blocked, they are missing from the comparison entirely.
k:U5:behebung: Keep saved scenarios as shared state (useSyncExternalStore).
k:U6:text: One-year warnings appear in the chart without an area, multi-year ones lose half a year at each edge. The warning lights are computed twice per frame.
k:U6:behebung: Numeric year axis with ±0.5 year margin; compute warning lights once and pass them on.
k:U7:text: The tabs have no arrow-key control and no linked panels. The selected row in the backtest is not announced to screen readers. Save messages may not be announced the first time. Saving under an existing name overwrites without warning.
k:U7:behebung: WAI-ARIA tabs pattern; aria-pressed; keep a live region mounted; ask before overwriting.
k:U8:text: The view lists effect sizes but not the thresholds of the situation classification (e.g. the risk premium tipping threshold of 3 pp), although the spec requires all registry entries.
k:U8:behebung: Add thresholds as a separate section.
k:M17:text: Bank rescues 2008–2010, stimulus packages and the Covid aid beyond the shock table raise actual debt strongly. The model lacks them, so the debt ratio in the backtest is about 20 pp too low.
k:M17:behebung: Partly fixed (phase 3a): financial transactions as a lever, German history set. Debt in the backtest nevertheless stays too low (U 1.25); the other special measures count as responses to rare major events and do not belong in the standard model. Since Spec 13.6 the model can compute a bank rescue itself (basic setting “Housing and banks”, off by default); in the backtest the 2008–2010 rescue remains a set path, because the German losses came from US securities.
k:D8:titel: Hand-set values for the USA and Japan unchecked
k:D8:text: Tax rates and bases, pension parameters, energy mix, net foreign assets, central bank holdings and interest rates for the USA and Japan are set from expert knowledge. Since spec 13.1 the Kalman filter confirms the NAIRU and productivity trend of the USA and Japan's NAIRU (hand-set value within the band). Japan's productivity trend (estimated −0.08) stays hand-set by judgement (distance to the IMF).
k:D8:behebung: Check against BEA, SSA, Fed, Cabinet Office, BoJ, MHLW; same pattern as D1.
k:M18:titel: Pension adjustment under national law missing
k:M18:text: The USA cuts benefits automatically when the Social Security trust fund is exhausted (expected around 2033); Japan lowers benefits via the macro slide. The model only knows the German contribution adjustment; for the USA and Japan it is off, and the increase ends up in the deficit.
k:M18:behebung: Benefit adjustment as a second automatic mechanism (pension level instead of contribution), with the legal default per country.
k:M19:titel: Exchange rate to the euro fixed
k:M19:text: Euro amounts (CO₂ price, integration costs, subsidies) are converted at a fixed rate; world energy prices apply to all countries in euros.
k:M19:behebung: Link the rate to the model's real exchange rate.
k:T4:text: There are no historical policy and world paths yet for the USA and Japan.
k:T4:behebung: History files for US/JP following the pattern of DE-historie.json.
k:U9:text: Changing the country replaces the address instead of adding a history entry. “Back” in the browser therefore does not return to the previous country.
k:U9:behebung: pushState on change and a popstate listener.
k:U10:titel: Migration slider up to 3,000 thousand for all countries
k:U10:text: The range was extended for the USA and now also applies to Germany and Japan.
k:U10:behebung: Make ranges overridable per country in the hand file.
k:D9:titel: Japan's government debt lower than expected
k:D9:text: The fetched IMF series shows about 207% of GDP for Japan in 2025; the World Economic Outlook rather says 230–240%. Possibly a different definition or vintage.
k:D9:behebung: Check the series and definition (gross, central/general government); if needed, a hand value with source.
k:D10:titel: Actual pension spending from hand-set values
k:D10:text: The actual series of pension spending 2000–2025 (% of GDP) in the backtest comes from hand-set values based on OECD SOCX and the German pension insurer, not from a fetched series.
k:D10:behebung: Fetch the series from OECD SOCX or the pension insurance report and replace it.
k:M20:titel: Foreign trade drifts in the long run
k:M20:text: Since phase 3a exports follow world demand (elasticity 1) and imports follow own income (1.5), exports pull intermediate imports along (25%), foreign assets raise spending (4% a year) and lift the equilibrium rate (1% per 1 pp of GDP, calibrated). Because world demand grows permanently by 2.5% going forward while Germany and Japan grow much more slowly, the export ratio (Germany 2075 about 68% of GDP), foreign assets (Germany 216%, Japan 253% of GDP) and above all the real exchange rate (Germany 2050 +55%, 2075 a good doubling; Japan 2.6-fold) still grow. The current account stays plausible (Germany and Japan 4–8% of GDP, USA around −2%). The strong appreciation lowers inflation by 0.1–0.3 pp and raises the debt ratio in 2075 by up to 12 pp. A guard test over 100 years prevents it from getting worse.
k:M20:behebung: Competitors' catch-up as its own mechanism (market shares, Krugman's 45-degree rule) or trade-weighted instead of global demand per country; then a weaker equilibrium rate again.
k:T5:titel: Minor findings from the phase 3a review
k:T5:text: (1) Life expectancy in the backtest keeps the last annual change after the last data year. (2) If the start year of an actual series is missing, there is no benchmark and the verdict is “no data”. (3) An exactly straight actual series has a band of width zero; the test named “is zero” checks 0. (4) If the model returns NaN, the view shows “∞” instead of an error. (5) If imports are less than a quarter of exports, the first year misses the starting value (not reachable today). (6) If the current account is missing in the data year, the remainder silently becomes 0. (7) The test “no hurdle test without history” cannot fail for the USA and Japan; pension spending passes the hurdle only narrowly (U 0.99). (8) The field defizitNom contains the financial transactions.
k:T5:behebung: Fix individually when the code is touched; suggestions in the phase 3a review report.
k:M21:titel: Model inflation too high in the backtest
k:M21:text: From 2004 to 2018 model inflation is about 1 pp above actual. That raises nominal GDP, lowers the debt ratio and makes Germany dearer in real terms within the euro area. Tying expectations to the euro-area path helped debt but worsened growth (U 0.69 → 0.96) and was rejected.
k:M21:behebung: Examine wage and price setting (wage restraint 2003–2008) as its own mechanism.
k:M22:titel: Policy rate jumps at the start
k:M22:text: Japan starts with 3.2% inflation. The central bank rule raises the policy rate in one step from 0.4 to 3.5% in 2026. This is followed by a credit impulse of −5% of GDP in 2027 and an output gap of −3.2% in 2028: without shocks, Japan shows one recession year (−1.2% per capita). Since phase 3b this is visible as a situation; before, a single negative year only showed as “stagnating”. The test “rare without shocks” therefore allows at most one such year per country.
k:M22:behebung: Interest-rate smoothing in the central bank rule (the rate follows the rule only partly each year), then set the test back to “never”.
k:M23:titel: USA: growth and government debt against CBO, Fed and IMF
k:M23:text: Sanity check 28 Sept 2026. Previously the model computed about 1.0% real growth for the USA (2026–2035); CBO sees 2.1% (2026–2030) and 1.8% (2031–2036), the Fed 2.0% in the long run. The cause was productivity, not labour supply (model −0.1% a year, CBO near zero). Fixed via two hand-set values: capital coefficient 3.2 → 2.75 (otherwise depreciation 19.2 instead of 16.3% of GDP according to BEA) and TFP trend 0.8 → 1.0 (= productivity frontier). Since then 1.6% (2026–2035). Still open: (0) Starting deficit checked: revenue and spending (IMF Public Finances in Modern History, 2024) give an 8.0% deficit, the current WEO says 7.9% (Germany 2.6 vs 2.7%, Japan 1.5 vs 1.7%). An earlier comparison with 7.3% was based on an outdated WEO vintage. Still open: the IMF expects the US deficit to improve to 6.8% in 2025 and 7.5% in 2026, the model stays at about 8%; it does not know policy from 2025 (above all tariff revenue). A lower effective interest rate (2.7 instead of 3.0%) was tested and rejected: it only shifts spending from interest to the primary deficit and raises debt in 2055. (1) Debt is computed as general government gross debt (IMF, 124%), CBO uses federal debt held by the public (101%); the primary deficit for general government is about 1.5 pp lower than CBO's (federal 2.6%). The two debt paths are therefore not directly comparable. (2) The spending structure differs but roughly balances out: health stays fixed (CBO: Medicare rises to 5.5% of GDP), pensions rise to 7.0 instead of 6.0% by 2055, revenue stays fixed (CBO: +1.3 pp). (3) The debt brake (Bohn 1998) saves about 4% of GDP by 2055; CBO computes under current law without counter-steering. (4) Migrants find work following a curve from German refugee research (half-life 5 years), probably too slow for the USA; at the same time net migration (1.1 m) is probably above the CBO assumption. The two errors roughly cancel out in labour supply.
k:M23:behebung: Model tariff revenue in the budget; link health spending to ageing; revenue with progression (bracket creep); set integration speed and net migration for the USA jointly against BLS and the CBO Demographic Outlook; depreciation rate per country instead of global.
k:M24:text: Sanity check 28 Sept 2026. Without shocks, Germany (0.0% 2026–2035) and Japan (0.1%) grew much more slowly than the estimates (Germany about 0.4%, Bank of Japan 0.5–1.0%) because labour supply fell by about 1% a year. Partly fixed: a participation trend per country (Germany +0.3 pp a year for 12 years, Japan +0.4 pp for 10 years) captures the rising participation of older people and women and only works forward. Since then 0.24% (Germany) and 0.35% (Japan), still below the estimates. Open: (1) migrants work too rarely, after years only a quarter to a third of working-age migrants. A faster curve for labour migration added only +0.05 pp of growth and worsened the backtest (debt U 1.31, trade); rejected. The bottleneck lies rather in the target employment rate, the mix of routes and counting (B1). (2) Work beyond retirement age is missing as a quantity of its own; in Japan it is roughly contained in the trend.
k:M24:behebung: Check migrant employment against the microcensus and OECD integration indicators (target, mix of routes, share of children); employment beyond retirement age as a rate. Every change must pass the German backtest.
k:M25:titel: Effect sizes for order and commodities only partly checked
k:M25:text: Update 4a computes rule of law, state ownership, price controls, central bank financing, directed lending, commodities and managed currency with literature values. Update 4c checks them against nine case files (eight cases): the direction is right everywhere; hyperinflation and emigration (Venezuela), East Germany's productivity gap (56% of West Germany in 1989) and Argentina's black market also match the order of magnitude. Calibrated: directed lending → capital efficiency 0.3 → 0.5 (USSR; the test therefore checks the calibration target, not independent evidence). In addition, four corrections from the cases: commodity revenue at the real exchange rate (divisor at least 0.8), commodity volume in output (also works upward: output 200 lifts Russia's GDP by about 11% at once, with no capital needed), price controls collapse under high inflation, a negative real rate counts at most down to −5% above 25% inflation. The G7 and China compute unchanged as a result, Russia minimally differently (growth 2026–2031 still 1.03%). The other effect sizes remain literature values; emigration due to a pure economic slump is deliberately missing. The cases are set up with roughly set paths (sources per case file).
k:M25:behebung: Check the cases' paths against annual data; close gaps M3, M26, M27.
k:M26:titel: Foreign-currency shortage and import compression missing
k:M26:text: When a source of foreign currency disappears (oil price and output in Venezuela from 2014, Soviet aid to Cuba in 1991), in reality imports of intermediate goods are missing and production collapses. The model does not know this channel: Venezuela loses −11% per capita in 2013–2020 (observed about −70%), Cuba −4% in 1990–1993 (observed −35%). The direction is right, the magnitude is not.
k:M26:behebung: Intermediate imports in production; scarce foreign currency (current account, black market) limits them. Then turn the “known gap (M26)” tests into normal tests.
k:M27:titel: Stagnation from an unchanging order missing
k:M27:text: The order only works via the deviation from the country standard, so that the baseline runs stay exactly the same. A planned economy whose order does not change therefore does not lose momentum over time in the model: the USSR keeps growing at 2.4% per capita in the 1980s (observed below 1%, Easterly/Fischer 1995). The slow decline from the order itself (falling innovative power, wrong incentives) is missing.
k:M27:wirkung: medium (long runs with a planned economy)
k:M27:behebung: Productivity trend dependent on the level of the order, neutralised for the baseline runs through the country standard; test “known gap (M27)”.
k:D11:titel: China and Russia: hand-set values unchecked, official figures with reservations
k:D11:text: Hand-set values (order, tax rates, pensions, commodities, capital stock) are set from expert knowledge. Some spending items are below the registry's lower bound and sit at the bound (China: health, family, net migration; Russia: pension level, wage replacement, health). China's growth is considered smoothed, the hidden debt (35% of GDP) is an IMF estimate. Since 2022 Russia no longer publishes parts of its data; the OECD yield is missing, substitute 12% (see below). Both compute with a managed currency; the policy rate starts at the start-year real rate (Russia 8%) and approaches the world real rate over about ten years. Demand, credit and shadow rate are measured against the same path. The Russian substitute yield (12% instead of about 15% during the war in 2025) keeps the term premium at about 1 pp. Growth is calibrated against the IMF for 2026–2031 (TFP trend China 2.3, Russia 0.55%). Towards the end of the century, debt crises push the black-market premium above 5%.
k:D11:behebung: Check hand-set values against IMF Article IV, OECD and World Bank; open registry bounds for emerging economies. (The cases from Update 4c check the mechanics, not these hand-set values.)
k:M28:titel: Stabilisation via an exchange-rate anchor missing
k:M28:text: With very high inflation the anchor of expectations is almost gone in the model; a falling inflation target then does not get through. Russia stabilised in 1995–1997 via an exchange-rate corridor (inflation 197 → 15%); in the model it stays at 150%. The same applies to any stabilisation after a hyperinflation (currency board Argentina 1991, Bulgaria 1997).
k:M28:behebung: A credible exchange-rate anchor as a lever that re-anchors expectations; test “known gap (M28)”.
k:T6:titel: Minor findings from the phase 3b review
k:T6:text: (1) Edge cases exactly on the threshold are not tested for 2.5% (boom), a 0.5 pp debt rise, exactly 90% of the peak and exactly target + 2.2 pp inflation. (2) The crisis explanation in the narrative reads the premium threshold from the registry default, the classification uses the country value; the same today because no country overrides the threshold. (3) Three years with a tiny decline per capita (−0.01% each) yield a depression, although each year on its own would be stagnation; this is what the spec says (“negative”). (4) The info texts on the risk premium state “3 percentage points” as fixed instead of taking it from the registry.
k:T6:behebung: (1) add four edge-case tests; (2) use standardWert("schwelle.aufschlag", land); (3) check whether negative years should count only below a small threshold; (4) generate the text from the registry.

k:U11:titel: Minor findings from the review of the English version
k:U11:text: (1) A language switch rebuilds the view: selected year, open chart, comparison partner, selection in the effect network and the list of adopted packages (undo) are lost; the scenario stays. (2) In English there is sometimes a space before the percent sign (“3.2 %”), sometimes not. (3) Measure names are capitalised mid-sentence in English (“after 10 years Economic prosperity per capita …”). (4) Source abbreviations such as “IWF” stay German. (5) “1 children per woman”: units lack a singular form.
k:U11:behebung: (1) Keep year, chart and adopted packages above the rebuild; (2) percent format via Intl per language; (3) lower case mid-sentence or sentence templates per measure; (4) source abbreviations per language; (5) units with a singular form.
Konjunkturpakete, Großprogramme, Reforme: stimulus packages, large programmes, reforms and austerity by the government
v:grund.politik:name: Policy
v:grund.politik:erklaerung: Fixed: the levers stay as set. Reacting: under prolonged weakness and a tight budget the government decides. It does not choose the best solution but between three options; you can switch at every point.
v:politik.steueranteil:name: Consolidation through taxes
v:politik.steueranteil:erklaerung: If the government has to consolidate, this share comes from higher income tax and VAT, the rest from spending cuts.
v:politik.steueranteil:kanal: the mix of consolidation between taxes and cuts
v:politik.kuerzeAlles:name: Cuts to defence and education too
v:politik.kuerzeAlles:erklaerung: On: if the other cuts are not enough, the government also cuts defence and education.
v:politik.kuerzeAlles:kanal: further cuts when the budget is tight
v:politik.risiko:name: Political risk after crises
v:politik.risiko:erklaerung: On: after a crisis the risk premium rises for some years because governments fragment and reforms stall.

k:M29:titel: Policy reacts by stylised rules, with a tendency towards high debt
k:M29:text: Since spec 13.13 the government chooses at each trigger (lasting weakness, tight budget) between three options: holding on to power (spending, debt rule halved, hidden revenue), direction (a large programme or burden-sharing according to the structure of the country) and an uncomfortable decision (part of the matching package, watered down, partly rolled back later). A rule without chance says which one it probably chooses; the user can switch. Stylised: (1) The rules are assumptions; they match the pattern of German history in part (2010 stimulus after the crisis, 2014 pension at 63 and 2025 special fund yes; 2003 Agenda 2010 no, because weakness had lasted only two years). (2) Direction follows the structure of the country from the start values (welfare spending, energy imports, current account): an approximation that fits Canada, China and Russia poorly. (3) The reversal rate (30%) rests on few cases; the election-year effect is not visible in the app's data and is set to 0. (4) The election cycle is fixed; early elections are unknown to the model. (5) The government sees only growth, unemployment and the budget, no majorities or coalitions. (6) Since the M29 fix the base model knows the budget plans until 2031: the overall balance follows the IMF in 2026–2031, after that the measures stay (switch “Budget plans until 2031”). The plan is calibrated, not built from individual measures; it also absorbs what the model otherwise gets wrong (above all the too steep rise in pensions until 2031). Only the part beyond that affects demand. Debt 2050 (policy reacts): France 149, Italy 256, Germany 123, United Kingdom 116. The gap to the IMF in 2031 falls on average over the nine countries from 10.5 to 5.0 points; what remains is mainly growth that is too weak (Germany +4, Japan +12, Canada +4, Italy +2.5) and in China the IMF stock-flow adjustment (−13.5). After 2031 pensions drive debt: they rise with the ratio of pensioners to employees at a fixed level (Italy 2050 about 25% of GDP, the Ageing Report sees about 16). Debt crisis by 2050 in the random runs: France 6%, Italy 33%, Germany 44%. (7) In the United Kingdom and France the main line lies below the band of the runs: shocks trigger more decisions in the runs than on the smooth line, and each one costs (United Kingdom 2050: line 91, band 102 to 139). Since the gliding investment anchor, Germany lies inside the band. Whether that is too pessimistic only a comparison with cases can show.
k:M29:wirkung: high (debt, crisis shares and growth of the base runs)
k:M29:behebung: Check the rules against cases (Italy 2011/12, Japan 2013, Germany 2003–2005); set pension spending of all countries against the Ageing Report and national projections (M1), then growth against the IMF (Japan: rate jump in the first year, T8 and D12); reconsider the structure assignment for Canada, China and Russia.
k:M34:titel: Investment ratio in the hindcast still 3 to 5 points too high
k:M34:text: Since Spec 13.5 Part B investment follows capacity utilisation, and the interest rate acts more weakly (0.15 instead of 0.6). In the hindcast for Germany 2000–2025 the model then computed an investment ratio of 23 to 27%; the measured values were 18 to 23%. Cause: the ratio stayed anchored forever at the start-year ratio, in the hindcast 24.0% in the last year of the construction boom after reunification; a ratio of about 21% would have held the capital stock. The capital-output ratio therefore rose from 3.0 to 3.6, and growth at 1.17% lay above the measured 1.01%.
k:M34:wirkung: medium (hindcast Germany: capital stock and growth too high)
k:M34:behebung: Let the anchor of the investment ratio glide to the ratio that holds the capital stock.
k:M35:titel: Public capital stock: only as a deviation
k:M35:text: The lever “Public investment” (Spec 13.5 Part B) only computes the deviation from the path with today's investment. A country that already invests too little today loses nothing in the baseline: Germany's net investment was 0.1% of GDP in 2000–2023, France's 0.6%, and both simply continue in the model. Since the small items the deviation is measured against the actual stock (IMF Investment and Capital Stock Dataset, 2019: Germany 44% of GDP, Japan 121%); with a fixed effect size of 0.1 (Bom/Ligthart 2014) each euro yields more where the stock is small. Projecting the stock forward with today's investment would hinge on the depreciation rate (2.5 to 4.5%), which would move the baselines more than anything else; that remains open. The model does not distinguish between roads, schools and administrative buildings. A debt-financed investment does not pay for itself: +1% of GDP permanently raises GDP per capita in Germany by 2.5% by 2050 (previously 1.6), and debt by 17 pp. For China the IMF includes state enterprises; the stock is converted to general-government investment. In the hindcast for Germany the measured investment path worsens government debt, because the cuts of 2004–2007 further lower a debt level that is already too low in the model.
k:M35:wirkung: medium (baselines underestimate the cost of a maintenance backlog)
k:M35:behebung: Project the stock forward once depreciation per country is documented (Eurostat, BEA, Cabinet Office); check the effect size by type of investment.

k:M36:titel: Random shocks: few cases, same frequency for all countries
k:M36:text: The random runs (Spec 13.4) draw four types: financial crisis, oil price shock, pandemic, war in the neighbourhood. Estimated are the financial crisis (25 crises in 18 countries 1970–2020; the risk rises with the credit gap) and the oil price shock (counted on the oil price series since 1946: 3.9 to 5.8% per year, set to 5%). War in the neighbourhood (1.5%) is an assumption from a handful of cases, the pandemic (2%) comes from a study. All countries have the same frequencies and the same shock paths; only the demand loss from energy shocks follows net energy imports since the small items (producers lose no demand; Canada and the USA also get no revenue, which only Russia has through its commodity sector). Shocks occur independently of each other. Trade war, war with own participation, supply stop and unknown types are not drawn. With “Housing and banks” on, the random crisis bursts a bubble, which the model does not do by itself (M31); the price fall remains smaller than measured (USA: median 13% over five years, measured 37%).
k:M36:wirkung: medium (width of the band, share of runs with a debt crisis)
k:M36:behebung: Frequency of wars in the neighbourhood per country once a case count exists; commodity sector for Canada and the USA.
k:M37:titel: Policy reacts: main line and random runs read “years in a row” differently
k:M37:text: The government reacts after several weak years in a row (Spec 13.10). On the smooth main line this applies literally. In the random runs (Spec 13.4) three of the last five years suffice for weakness (stimulus package) and five of the last seven (reform), because growth jumps from year to year there; saving stays literal; otherwise a reform would come in only 23% of runs in Germany, while on the main line it comes in 2032. Consequence: in countries close to the threshold the government reforms in most random runs but never on the main line (Japan 90%, United Kingdom 85%, Canada 97% of runs). There the line lies at the edge of the band (Japan: debt in 2050 on the line 261%, median of runs 214%). The literal rule is also sensitive on the main line: with the rule of the random runs a reform would come in Canada in 2031, and debt in 2050 would be 100 instead of 125% of GDP.
k:M37:wirkung: medium (position of the line within the band; Canada, Japan, United Kingdom)
k:M37:behebung: One rule for both: measure weakness by the mean of several years; then recompute the baselines and the before/after of 13.10.
k:M30:titel: Credit impulse oscillates in a sawtooth under deflation
k:M30:text: In the calibration case Argentina 1992–2002 the credit impulse jumps year by year between about −28 and +16 pp of GDP, growth accordingly between −13 and +10%. Suspected cause, not verified: under deflation and a strong denominator effect deleveraging overshoots, and credit catches up the year after. The asymmetry from Spec 13.5 part A deepens the down years somewhat, so Argentina now reaches the state “crisis” in 2002. The baseline runs of the nine countries do not show the sawtooth.
k:M30:behebung: Smooth deleveraging (spread over several years) and test against Argentina and Japan in the 1990s; together with Spec 13.6.
k:D12:titel: Estimated starting values: end-of-sample values uncertain, neutral rate not wired in
k:D12:text: Since spec 13.1 a Kalman filter estimates the productivity trend, NAIRU, output gap and neutral real interest rate for each country. (1) The neutral real rate is only shown. In the model it appears as the world real rate in the Taylor rule and as the starting-year real rate in the demand reference; using it would change the mechanics. (2) An estimate replaces the hand-set value only if that value lies outside its band; 11 of 18 hand-set values are confirmed this way, only Canada's productivity trend is replaced (0.38 instead of 0.7). (3) The estimate is least certain at the end of the series, and the inflation observations for 2021–2023 are left out (supply shock). Where an estimate moves growth in 2026–2030 more than 0.3 pp further from the IMF, the hand-set value stays by judgement: NAIRU in Canada and China, productivity trend in Japan. The judgement carries no date and must be rechecked by hand after new data. (4) Russia: the filter does not fit the data (κ 3.1), all hand-set values stay.
k:D12:wirkung: medium (starting values, growth in the first years)
k:D12:behebung: Base the Taylor anchor and the demand reference on one common, country-specific neutral rate (decision in 13.5); energy price as a variable in the inflation equation instead of leaving out the shock years; quarterly data.

r:zinskurve:name: Yield curve (10 years minus policy rate)
r:zinskurve:beschreibung: Gap between the 10-year yield and the policy rate. Below zero the yield curve is inverted.
r:zinskurve:info:0: The yield on ten-year government bonds minus the policy rate, in percentage points. In a currency union the euro-area policy rate counts.
r:zinskurve:info:1: Normally the long yield is higher. If it is below, markets expect falling rates, usually because a slowdown is coming.
r:zinskurve:info:2: In the USA almost every recession since 1970 was preceded by an inverted yield curve (Estrella/Mishkin 1998), most recently 2006/07 and 2019.
r:zinskurve:info:3: The model computes the yield and the policy rate anyway; the curve is just their difference and feeds back into nothing. With a managed currency the state sets the policy rate; there is no warning light there.
r:kreditluecke:name: Credit gap
r:kreditluecke:beschreibung: Gap between private debt and its long-term trend. Above 10 pp a banking crisis looms.
r:kreditluecke:info:0: Private debt (% of GDP) minus its long-term trend, in percentage points (the BIS credit-to-GDP gap).
r:kreditluecke:info:1: When credit grows much faster than the economy, bubbles form. The gap is the best known early indicator of banking crises.
r:kreditluecke:info:2: Before the 2008 financial crisis it was far above 10 pp in the USA, Spain and Ireland. Basel III links the countercyclical capital buffer to it.
r:kreditluecke:info:3: Trend as at the BIS: one-sided HP filter (past data only) with λ = 1,562.5 for annual data, started with IMF private debt since 1950. Feeds back into nothing.

k:T8:titel: Minor findings from the review of 13.1 and 13.2
k:T8:text: 13.1 Kalman: (1) The filter always treats the first 3 years as burn-in; κ therefore comes out slightly too small (Germany 1.61 instead of 1.74). (2) A judgement against an estimate (schaetzungAus) carries no date and stays in force unchecked after new data. (3) The band of the productivity trend leaves out the uncertainty of labour growth. (4) If real growth ends before the data year, the estimate still carries the data year (not the case today). (5) An invalid neutral rate without a value shows as "0.00 %" (not the case today). (6) The hand-set version of the countries is built in the browser needlessly; the estimated series are in the bundle (about 7.5 KB per country). 13.2 early warning: (7) Japan shows an inverted yield curve in 2026 because the policy rate jumps from 0.4 to 3.5 % in the first model year; a start jump, not a signal. (8) The info text of the credit gap says "since 1950"; some series start later (Japan 1964, China 1985). (9) In the backtest the credit gap starts at 0 in 2000; a start from data up to 2000 would be possible (gap +15, then a light in 2001 instead of 2010). (10) With hyperinflation the yield-curve chart becomes unreadably large. (11) The yield curve is colour-neutral in the comparison; a curve that is no longer inverted does not count as good.
k:T8:behebung: (1) count only steps without a diffuse share; (2) store the judgement with a year and drop it for a new data year; (7) suppress the yield-curve light in the first model year; (8) "since the start of the IMF series"; (9) credit start in the backtest from data up to the start year; (10) limit the display; the rest as needed.

v:banken.sicherheiten:name: House prices → credit (collateral)

v:banken.lgd:name: Loss per defaulted loan
v:banken.lgd:erklaerung: This share of a bad loan is lost when it is written off.
v:banken.abschreibung:name: Write-off of bad loans, fast rescue
v:banken.abschreibung:erklaerung: This share of bad loans is written off each year and reduces equity.
v:banken.abschreibungZoegernd:name: Write-off of bad loans, hesitant rescue
v:banken.abschreibungZoegernd:erklaerung: Bad loans stay on the books; the losses come later, and correspondingly fewer loans recover.
v:banken.heilung:name: Bad loans are serviced again
v:banken.heilung:erklaerung: This share of bad loans recovers each year without a loss.
v:banken.klemme:name: Credit crunch
v:banken.klemme:erklaerung: If equity falls more than a tenth below today's value (or below a lowered requirement), banks cut lending: per percentage point below, by this many percent of the stock, each year half the way there, at most 10% a year.
v:banken.kapitalkosten:name: More equity → lending rate
v:banken.kapitalkosten:erklaerung: Each percentage point of additional required equity makes credit this much more expensive.
v:banken.staatBank:name: Sovereign-bank loop
v:banken.staatBank:erklaerung: When the yield rises, banks lose market value on their government bonds. 0 = off.
v:schwelle.bankMindest:name: Bank rescue: equity below this share of its starting value
v:schwelle.bankMindest:erklaerung: With a fast rescue, the state tops equity up to the target below this level.
v:schwelle.hausluecke:name: House price gap above
v:schwelle.hausluecke:erklaerung: Gap between the real house price and its one-sided HP trend. Together with the credit gap it warns better than either alone.
v:banken.rendite:name: Return on bank equity
v:banken.rendite:erklaerung: Profit before exceptional write-offs, at the country's inflation target; with higher inflation it rises along. It absorbs losses first and rebuilds equity after a crisis; whatever exceeds the target is paid out.
k:M31:titel: A bubble does not burst by itself
k:M31:text: Since Spec 13.6 a housing boom from cheap money arises inside the model: in the cases USA 2000–2014 and Japan 1985–2005 house prices and credit rise with the measured monetary policy almost as measured (USA 2006 +49% instead of +55%, Japan 1990 +33% instead of +34%). The turning point is missing. Without a set trigger, US house prices hardly fall after 2008, and the zero interest rates after the crisis set off a new boom in the model (Japan after 1995: house prices quadruple instead of −40%). What is missing is the balance-sheet recession (households and firms repay debt despite zero rates), deflation and the loss of confidence in financial markets. In the cases USA, Spain and Ireland the financial crisis is therefore set as a shock. The warning lamps show the danger; the moment of the burst is determined by a shock.
k:M31:wirkung: high (banks on: crises need a trigger; after a crisis the housing market recovers too fast)
k:M31:behebung: Add a balance-sheet recession: after a fall in prices debtors repay for years regardless of the interest rate (Koo 2008). Since Spec 13.4 the trigger exists for the random runs (probability rises with the credit and house price gaps); on the main line it is still missing. Then re-test against USA, Spain, Ireland and Japan.
k:M32:text: One bank per country, no contagion between countries, equity unweighted and relative to its starting value. The bank only loses on domestic loans and government bonds; losses on securities (USA 2008) and on foreign business are missing. The state only rescues when half of the equity of the whole banking sector is gone. In reality the weakest banks fail earlier. Result in the calibration cases: USA 2008 no rescue (measured 4.5% of GDP, Laeven/Valencia 2018), Spain none (5.4%), Ireland 7% of GDP (37.6%). The sovereign-bank loop in Spain 2012 therefore does not arise. The opposite holds in Japan: banks there hold many government bonds, rising yields eat up their equity, and in the baseline with banks on they cut lending in 46 of 50 years. The banks' share of government debt and housing wealth per country are unverified hand values. The basic setting “Housing and banks” is therefore off by default.
k:M32:wirkung: high with banks on (cost of a banking crisis to the state too small); none when off
k:M32:behebung: Split the banking sector into two parts (sound and weak banks) or calibrate the rescue threshold on the cases; model securities losses via the fall in house prices; look up the hand values in the original sources (IMF, Arslanalp/Tsuda).
k:M33:titel: Housing boom in the wrong places: Spain and Ireland too small, Germany too large
k:M33:text: In the case Spain 1998–2016 private debt rises in the model from 92 to 99% of GDP by 2007, measured to 213%; house prices rise by 16% instead of 120%. In the case Ireland 2002–2015 house prices fall from 2003 on, because in the starting year they were already 30% above the long-run ratio to income; measured they rose another 46% until 2007. What is missing is the capital inflow from the euro area (banks funded themselves abroad), immigration into construction and inflation above the euro average, which pushed down the real interest rate. The opposite holds in the German hindcast 2000–2025 with banks on: from low euro interest rates the model computes a housing boom (+63% by 2008), whereas measured prices fell by 14% (overhang from the building boom after reunification, weak incomes). The house price lamp lights up in 2005–2008, banks cut credit from 2011, and the rise in interest rates in 2022 triggers a rescue of 4.5% of GDP via government bonds. Growth, inflation and unemployment fit worse (Theil's U 0.69 → 0.81, 0.79 → 0.84, 0.53 → 0.59).
k:M33:wirkung: medium (only with banks on; countries in a currency union with capital inflows)
k:M33:behebung: Capital inflow within the currency union as a source of credit (the current-account deficit funds credit); check the country's inflation above the euro average in the upswing; then recalculate Spain and Ireland.

r:hauspreis:name: House prices (real)
r:hauspreis:beschreibung: Price of residential property without inflation, starting year = 100.
r:hauspreis:info:0: The price of houses and flats, adjusted for inflation. The starting year is 100.
r:hauspreis:info:1: The home is the largest asset of most households and the most important collateral for loans. When prices rise there is more credit; more credit pushes prices further.
r:hauspreis:info:2: In the USA real house prices rose by 55% in 2000–2006 and then fell by a third. In Spain they doubled by 2007; in Japan they fell by more than 40% after 1991. A rise in line with income is harmless.
r:hauspreis:info:3: A fundamental value follows income per capita and the real interest rate. The price returns there slowly, has momentum and rises with credit above normal. Share prices are left out on purpose: bubbles without credit cost little. The bursting of a bubble does not arise by itself in the model (criticism M31).
r:hausluecke:name: House price gap
r:hausluecke:beschreibung: Gap between the real house price and its long-term trend. Above 15% a bubble looms.
r:hausluecke:info:0: Real house price minus its long-term trend, in percent.
r:hausluecke:info:1: Credit-financed housing bubbles often end in banking crises. Together with the credit gap, the house price gap warns better than either alone (Borio/Drehmann 2009).
r:hausluecke:info:2: Above 15% counts as a warning signal. After a crash the gap can also be high because the trend has followed the crash: then it is a recovery, not a bubble.
r:hausluecke:info:3: Trend as for the credit gap: one-sided HP filter (past data only), started with the BIS real house prices. Feeds back on nothing.
r:bankKapital:name: Bank equity
r:bankKapital:beschreibung: The banks' own money per 100 lent. The buffer against losses.
r:bankKapital:info:0: Bank equity in percent of the balance sheet, unweighted. In the model the whole country is a single bank.
r:bankKapital:info:1: Losses from bad loans first hit equity. Once it is used up, the state steps in or the bank cuts lending. More equity does not prevent crises but makes them milder (Jordà/Richter/Schularick/Taylor 2021). In return credit becomes slightly more expensive.
r:bankKapital:info:2: If the ratio falls more than a tenth below today's value, banks cut lending. Below half, the state tops it up under a fast rescue.
r:bankKapital:info:3: Previous year plus profit minus write-offs on bad loans minus price losses on government bonds. Anything above the target is paid out. Losses on securities and abroad are missing; rescues therefore turn out too small (criticism M32).
r:npl:name: Bad loans
r:npl:beschreibung: Share of bank loans that are no longer serviced.
r:npl:info:0: Loans on which interest or repayment has been overdue for more than 90 days, in percent of all bank loans.
r:npl:info:1: Bad loans are written off and eat up bank equity. If they stay on the books for long, banks lend little for years (Japan in the 1990s).
r:npl:info:2: 1 to 3% is normal. In the USA it was about 5% in 2010, in Spain about 9% in 2013, in Ireland 26%.
r:npl:info:3: The inflow rises with unemployment above the structural rate, with falling house prices and with debt service above the threshold. Part recovers, part is written off; more slowly under a hesitant rescue.

v:wachstum.investElastizitaet:erklaerung: Until Spec 13.5 part B this was 0.6. With that the model computed an investment ratio of 28 to 30% in the German hindcast; measured it was 19 to 23%.
v:wachstum.akzelerator:name: Capacity utilisation → investment (accelerator)
v:wachstum.akzelerator:erklaerung: When plants are well utilised, firms invest more; in a recession they cancel investment. That is why a crisis costs prosperity permanently (Cerra/Saxena 2008).
v:wachstum.investAnpassung:name: Investment returns to its normal level
v:wachstum.investAnpassung:erklaerung: Each year the investment rate closes this share of the gap to the rate that keeps the capital stock in line with GDP (depreciation plus trend growth times the capital-output ratio). Off: it stays at the start-year rate forever.
v:staat.investitionen:name: Public investment
v:staat.investitionen:erklaerung: Roads, railways, grids, schools and other state structures, before depreciation. Today's value is part of “Other government spending”; here the change counts.
v:staat.investitionen:kanal: the public capital stock and thereby productivity, in the short run also demand
v:staat.oeffKapital:name: Public capital stock → productivity
v:staat.oeffKapital:erklaerung: One percent more public capital raises productivity by this many percent. Only the deviation from the path with today's investment is computed, relative to the country's measured stock (IMF): where it is small, each euro yields more.
v:staat.oeffAbschreibung:name: Depreciation of the public capital stock
v:staat.oeffAbschreibung:erklaerung: Without investment, this share of the stock is lost each year.
